summary: RFC 4379 defines MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute, where the Router Alert Option must be set in the IP header of the Echo Request messages. This document explains how IPv6 Router Alert Option is used for these messages. It is now historic.

eli5.summary: Special test messages need a flag so routers look at them. This explains the flag for the newer addressing. It is historic.

questions: ipv6 router alert option mpls oam
what is the ipv6 router alert option for mpls oam
why does mpls lsp ping need router alert
subtitle: Allocates IPv6 Router Alert value 69 so MPLS ping and traceroute messages can be flagged for routers on IPv6.

tldr.problem: MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute (RFC 4379) require the Router Alert Option in the IP header, but IPv4 has a generic value for it and IPv6 had none that MPLS OAM tools could use.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines a new IPv6 Router Alert Option Value, 69, for MPLS OAM, and updates RFC 4379 to say it MUST be used in IPv6 headers.
tldr.outcome: The document is now marked Historic. It updated RFC 4379 and added one code point to the IANA registry of IPv6 Router Alert Option values.

today: RFC 7506 is marked Historic. It updated RFC 4379 and has not been obsoleted by another RFC.

sections.title: Why MPLS OAM Needs an IPv6 Value
sections.content:
A widely used MPLS Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) tool is the one in RFC 4379, often called MPLS LSP Ping/Traceroute. It requires the Router Alert Option (RAO) in the IP header. For example, the IP RAO MUST be set on an MPLS Echo Request, and on an Echo Reply when the Reply Mode is "Reply via an IPv4/IPv6 UDP packet with Router Alert".

For IPv4, RFC 2113 defines a generic Option Value of 0x0, assigned to "Router shall examine packet". For IPv6, RFC 2711 required the Value field to indicate a specific reason, and no value existed for MPLS LSP Ping/Traceroute or for general use. That made it impossible for MPLS OAM tools to use the IPv6 Router Alert mechanism.

As vendors began to implement MPLS on the IPv6 control plane, a value was needed in order to comply with RFC 4379.
sections.eli5: Test messages are supposed to carry a flag that says "routers, look at me." The flag existed for one kind of address but not the other, so the test messages could not follow the rules on the newer kind.

sections.title: The New IPv6 RAO Value
sections.content:
The document defines a new Option Value, 69, for the IPv6 RAO. It alerts transit routers to examine the packet more closely for MPLS OAM purposes. Any MPLS OAM application that needs its packets examined by a transit router can use it.

Within this document, the value is used by the MPLS Echo Request and MPLS Echo Reply for IPv6 messages, as RFC 4379 requires. The abstract adds that the value is applicable to all MPLS OAM and is not limited to LSP Ping/Traceroute.
sections.eli5: Number 69 is the new flag. Any test tool for these networks can attach it when it wants routers along the way to take a closer look.

sections.title: Update to RFC 4379
sections.content:
Sections 4.3 and 4.5 of RFC 4379 are updated. Every time the "Router Alert IP Option" is mentioned there, this text is appended: for an IPv4 header, the generic IPv4 RAO value 0x0 SHOULD be used; for an IPv6 header, the IPv6 RAO value (69) allocated through this document for MPLS OAM MUST be used.

So the IPv4 behavior is a recommendation, while the IPv6 behavior is a firm requirement.
sections.eli5: The old rulebook now gets one extra sentence: use the old flag on the old addresses, and use flag 69 on the new addresses.

sections.title: The IANA Registry Entry
sections.content: IANA has assigned a new code point under its "IPv6 Router Alert Option Values" registry, which RFC 2711 defined and RFC 5350 updated. The entry is value 69, description "MPLS OAM", reference RFC 7506.
sections.eli5: The official list of flag numbers got a new line saying that 69 means "MPLS test messages."

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document introduces no new security concerns beyond those already captured in RFC 4379 and RFC 6398, the latter of which expands the security considerations of RFC 2113 and RFC 2711.

IPv6 packets with the MPLS OAM RAO are encapsulated with an MPLS header and are not expected to be inspected by every label switched hop within an LSP. The RFC concludes that this value will be processed by the appropriate router and is not subject to the problem of being ignored, as described in Section 2.2 of RFC 7045.
sections.eli5: Adding this flag does not open any new doors for trouble. The messages travel wrapped up inside the MPLS network, so only the right routers are expected to read them.
